Lecture 2- Intro to Networking

A network is a system of interconnected computers that can share data, and possibly information, with each other.

These days we have access to networks by using:

  • telephone lines
  • cable lines
  • fiber optic lines
  • wireless
    • Bluetooth personal area networks
    • local Wi-Fi networks
    • cell phone towers
    • satellite systems

Types of networks

Plain Old Telephone System (POTS)

Alexander Graham Bell’s company, AT&T, had a monopoly on the telephone system in the United States.

A telephone switch is a device that connects two telephone lines together so that an audio connection can be made between two telephones.

Then, within the network, there was a large number of physically connected switches that were connected to each other kind of like how the internet is structured today.

When someone made a call, a path was established through the switches from the source to the destination.

A dedicated pathway was important because the data being sent through the network was audio data and it is

  • sensitive to delay
  • had to be sent in the order it was generated

Capacity was set aside on all of these switches for the duration of the call. This is called 'circuit switching'.

When the call was over, the circuit was torn down and the capacity was freed up for other calls.

Automated routing systems were invented by a funeral director named Almon Strowger in the 1890s. He was upset his funeral home business was losing business to a competitor whose wife was working as a telephone operator. The operator would not connect calls to Strowger's funeral home, so he invented an automated switch that would connect calls without the need for a human operator.

It took a while for automated switches to spread throughout the world.

Automated central switches are responsible for managing the connections.

The end terminals are quite dumb (think of the phones in your grandparents' houses connected to a wall).

Person Using a Rotary Phone (I have actually done this many, many times in my life).

The POTS system has the intelligence built into the network.

The internet relies on a similar network model (with machines called routers instead of switches) to exchange data across large distances, but the devices on the edge of the network have real intelligence built into them.

Since the end devices are smart, it typically doesn't make sense to reserve a dedicated pathway through the network for an entire communication session.

Instead, the internet uses 'packet switching', where data is broken into small packets and each packet is sent into the network on its own.

Each packet contains the destination address and the routers in the internet use it to decide where to send the packet next.

Packets from the same message may take different routes through the network.

They may arrive out of order, or not at all.

The destination machine reassembles the packets into the original message.

No capacity is reserved anywhere in the network.

This makes packet switching much more efficient than circuit switching for bursty computer data, where long silences are common between transmissions.

Circuit switching reserves a path before any data is sent (POTS).

Packet switching sends independently addressed packets with no reserved path (the internet).

Cell Phone System

With the POTS system, the end terminals never moved.

With the cell phone system, the end terminals are mobile.

They coordinate with the network to maintain a connection as they move from one cell to another.

There may be a 'hand off' between cell towers.

Cell phone towers are connected to each other through the internet rather than through the POTS network.

Audio data is digitized and sent across the internet in packets.

Cell phones utilize applications that use non-audio data as well so this packet based approach and internet infrastructure is more appropriate for cell phones.

Local Area Network (LAN)

A Local Area Network (LAN) is a collection of computers usually owned by the same company to share resources- information, printers, file servers, email servers, internet connection, etc.

Ethernet is the most common LAN technology.

These days we all have wireless mini-LANs in our homes 802.11 standards- WiFi.

Personal Area Network (PAN)

PAN's are usually wireless and connect devices that are in close proximity to each other.

Bluetooth is a common PAN technology with a range of about 10 meters.

Internet

The internet is a network of networks.

End systems reside at the edge of the internet.

Routers live inside the network.

There are some special routers at the edge of the network, known as Edge Routers or First Hop Routers.

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) maintain networks of routers and charge people to use them.

They connect to each other to widen their reach and form the internet.

Networked Application Architectures

With this infrastructure in place, we can create applications that use the internet to communicate with each other:

  • Web
  • Email
  • Online Banking (Bill Pay, etc)
  • E-commerce (Amazon, eBay, etc)
  • Web Conferencing (Zoom, WebEx, Google Meet, etc)
  • Video services (YouTube, Netflix, Hulu, etc)
  • Social Media (Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, TikTok, etc)
  • Gaming Servers
  • Live Streaming (Twitch, YouTube Live, etc)
  • Chat (WhatsApp, Messenger, Discord, etc)
  • File Transfer Protocol (FTP)
  • Telnet

Protocols

Protocols are used to assign meaning to the data that passes between two machines (sometimes with different hardware and operating systems).

Time request protocol

A request is asking for some information, and a reply is the response with that data or an indication that it wasn't possible to supply it.

A request always comes from a client and a reply always comes from a server.

Many protocols define the format of the messages and the order of handshake, requests, and replies.

HypterText Transfer Protocol (HTTP)

The HTTP protocol is used to request and reply for data on the web.

Formal standard- standardized by official industry or government body (like IEEE, ISO, ANSI, etc.)

De Facto standard- becomes a standard not because it has been approved by a standards organization but because it is widely used and recognized by the industry as being standard (like the QWERTY keyboard layout, Adobe PDF, etc.).

By adhering to recognized protocols different companies can compete for hardware and software customers.

Before standards you had to buy all equipment from same vendor.

Layering

Protocols define how systems interact with each other.

Communication protocols typically break the communication process into layers.

Each layer has a clearly defined interface that is agreed upon by vendors. It is easy to swap in and out different layers.

Each layer provides a service for the layer above. Think about our US Postal Service.

You (application 1)                 Me (application 2)
-------------------                 -------------------
Mail box                <->         Mail box
Mail Carrier            <->         Mail Carrier
Post Office             <->         Post Office
                physical transport

This group of layers reduces the complexity of the whole system by abstracting away the details of other layers into a simple interface while breaking a complex system into easily understandable chunks.

We can replace mail carriers with a suction tube and the other layers would remain unchanged.

Internet Protocol Stack

  • Application Layer (Web, email, ftp, telnet, ssh)

    • create applications that use the stack

  • Transport Layer (TCP, UDP)

    • provides service of transferring whole messages between client and server processes
    • Connection oriented- reliable transfer, flow control, congestion control
    • segmentation and reassembly
    • relies on IP to deliver TCP packets to remote machines

  • Network Layer (IP)

    • provides service of routing packets across internet
    • connectionless, not reliable
    • relies on data link layer to get data from one machine to another

  • Data Link Layer (Ethernet)

    • provides service of moving packets from one machine to another
    • decides when it is acceptable to use the medium
    • relies on physical layer to transmit the bits

  • Physical Layer

    • provides the service of transmitting bits across a medium

What Happens When You Request a Web Page?

Coming back to the original example of sending my name from machine A to machine B, let's look at what happens when you request a web page from your web browser.

When you type in a URL (Uniform Resource Locator) into your web browser, the following happens:

  1. Your web browser sends a request to a Domain Name System (DNS) server to resolve the domain name (e.g., www.google.com) to an IP address (e.g., 172.217.168.14)
    • Your internet service provider (ISP) usually provides the DNS server that your computer uses, but you can also configure your computer to use a different DNS server (e.g., Google Public DNS at 8.8.8.8)
  2. The DNS server responds with the IP address of the web server that hosts the website you requested.
    • The DNS server maps domain names to IP addresses using a distributed database that is maintained by a network of DNS servers around the world.
    • If your DNS server does not have the IP address stored, then it may need to request the mapping from other DNS servers to find the IP address associated with that domain name.
    • The DNS servers use the same protocols as the web servers to communicate with each other and with your web browser.
  3. Your web browser then creates and sends an HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) request to the web server at the IP address it received from the DNS server.
    • The HTTP request includes the type of request (e.g., GET, POST), the URL of the resource being requested, and any additional headers or data that may be needed for the request.
    • For HTTPS sites, the browser and server first establish an encrypted connection. We'll cover how later in the course.
  4. The HTTP request gets wrapped in a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) segment.
    • The HTTP request may be broken up into multiple packets if the request is large.
    • The packets may also be sent out of order, but the TCP software on the web server will be able to reassemble them correctly using sequence numbers that are included in the packets.
    • The request is guaranteed to be delivered to the web server. If there is a problem with the network and a packet is lost, then the stack will automatically retransmit the packet until it is successfully delivered (or it gives up and determines it is undeliverable).
  5. The TCP packet is wrapped in an IP (Internet Protocol) packet. This packet includes the source and destination IP addresses, as well as other information needed for routing the packet through the network.
    • IP is a routing protocol that is responsible for delivering packets from the source to the destination. It does this by using the IP addresses to determine the best path for the packet to take through the network.
    • Routers are the devices that forward packets based on their IP addresses. They use routing tables to determine the best path for the packet to take.
  6. An IP packet is wrapped in an Ethernet frame, a Wi-Fi frame, or some other established format for transmission over the network.
    • This moves data from one machine to another over a physical medium (e.g., copper wire, fiber optic cable, or wireless radio waves).
  7. All of these steps are repeated as the data moves through the network.
    • Eventually, when the HTTP request is delivered to the destination, the web server processes the request
    • The server responds with an HTTP response, perhaps finding a web page in the file system or generating the HTML dynamically
    • The server sends the response back as an HTTP message which includes the HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) content of the web page you requested.
    • Then, the response goes through the same process of being wrapped in TCP, IP, and Ethernet frames as it travels back to your web browser.
  8. When the originator receives the HTTP response, your web browser then renders the HTML content and displays the web page to you.

We are going to spend the rest of this section of the course learning about the details of how this all works.
